Very briefly, just one administrative matter, on Tuesday afternoon, Jesenka Residovic, the very competent case manager of the Boskoski Defence team, alerted the Prosecution to a point that perhaps needs some clarification, and it is simply this: That when myself and Ms. Valabhji referred to Exhibit 3P00379, on Tuesday, that it would be more precise to refer to the exhibits that we mentioned, for example, as 379.01 which was the Official Note of Mr. Tapuskovic, as well as 379.04. You will find this references at pages 11.015 of the transcript, as well as 11.004 and 11.005 of the transcript. utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honours, at pages 11.065 to 11.066, my colleague Mr. Mettraux referred you yesterday to the Trial Chamber judgement and the Appeals Chamber judgement in the Ntagurera case from the ICTR as support for the argument that Mr. Boskoski did not have effective control over the perpetrators charged in the indictment in these proceedings. But a careful reading of the Ntagurera judgements reveals that the circumstances of Mr. Boskoski in this case were dramatically different from the circumstances of the accused Bagambiki, the subject of the Ntagurera case. Mr. Bagambiki was a civilian prefect, an administrator of an area in Rwanda during the tragedy that occurred there in 1994. The perpetrators in that case, however, were gendarmerie, members of the Rwandan government's Ministry of Defence. Mr. Bagambiki possessed no legal authority or de facto authority over the gendarmerie, and it is for that reason that the trial judgement and the Appeals Chamber judgement found that Mr. Bagambiki did not exercise effective control over the perpetrators of the crimes in that case and found that no superior/subordinate relationship existed between the accused and the perpetrators. You'll fine this at paragraphs 633 to 639 of the Ntagurera trial judgement, and paragraphs 242 to 347 of the appeals judgement. In this case, Your Honours, the evidence demonstrates that Mr. Boskoski was the highest authority in the Ministry of Internal Affairs during 2001 and 2002. The evidence demonstrates that he exercised both de jure and de facto effective control over the regular and reserve police officers who perpetrated the crimes committed in the indictment, including the ability to punish them. Your Honours, my colleagues submit that there is no evidence to suggest that Zoran Krstevski, the advisor to Minister Boskoski in 2001, was present at OVR Cair on the 10th of August, 2001, nor evidence suggesting that he was an advisor at that time to the minister. But, Your Honours, the testimony on cross-examination of Defence expert witness, Professor Slagjana Taseva, corroborates M-052's testimony about the presence of Mr. Boskoski's advisor, Zoran Krstevski, with Mr. Tarculovski at OVR Cair on Friday afternoon, the 10th of August. Professor Taseva explained that an individual could advise the Macedonian government ministries without being a formal employee of that ministry. This at pages 9.787 to 9.790 of the transcript. My colleague Mr. Mettraux, at page 11,070, and my colleague Mr. Apostolski, at page 11.114, argued yesterday that no evidence exists that Mr. Tarculovski and Mr. Boskoski were together at Brace's house on the 12th of August. But a careful reading of the testimony of witness M-037, at pages 873 to 876, reveals that his evidence was that Mr. Tarculovski and Mr. Boskoski were present together at Brace's house on that Sunday afternoon. Starting at page 873, during the re-direct exam of Witness M-037, I read to the witness paragraph 14 of an investigator's note prepared by the Office of the Prosecutor, and I said to the witness: "And let me say, witness, as we discuss paragraph 14, if you see something that is not correct there, please tell us, because you're here to tell the truth." Then I said: "Let's turn to paragraph 14, please. During cross-examination, my colleague asked you about the presence of Mr. Boskoski near the Chinese wall, and what he understood or what he did not understand, what he was doing there. Then there was an objection from Ms. Residovic, which was overruled, and then I continued. At the bottom of page 874: "You see there under paragraph 14, in the English version, there's a letter "A" which stands for "answer," your answer. "And you say: 'The minister was there.' "And up above the question" - this is myself continuing - "And up above the question was related to a conversation between Ljube Boskoski and Johan Tarculovski. You continue your answer. "You say, after you say the minister was there, he was interested in the situation. 'I think he was speaking to the police commander Ljube Krstevski. Johan was aside. I assume Ljube Krstevski told Ljube Boskoski, told him about some arms that they have found with some terrorists. I assume that the minister asked Ljube Krstevski to see the weapons and the minister came and saw the weapons.'" Then I continued: "In your answer to the next question, after the investigator asked about why you used the term 'discretion' in a prior interview with the Office of the Prosecutor, you say: 'Johan was showing or pointing to the weapons,' and then, 'Johan was all the time standing aside. Ljube Krstevski and Ljube Boskoski were speaking, and Ljube Boskoski was asking for some explanation for the action.'" Then I asked: "Could you tell us, please, whether Ljube Boskoski got such an explanation at that time?" Answer from M-037: "From whom? Question: Well at the moment from Ljube Krstevski. Answer: When they were by the Hermeline. Question: Yes. Answer: I assume he got an answer during -- if he was able to get an answer during the ten seconds, but I will stress again, I think it was Ljube Krstevski. I'm not sure who that was." The only comment that M-037 wanted to make was to explain his uncertainty, whether Mr. Krstevski was present at that moment. He expressed no uncertainty about the presence of Mr. Tarculovski. It's also important on this same topic, Your Honour, to review the testimony of Mr. Boskoski's body-guard in 2001, Blagoja Jakovoski, about the presence of Mr. Tarculovski and Mr. Boskoski together at Brace's house in the afternoon of 12th August. As you will recall, Mr. Jakovoski accompanied Mr. Boskoski to Brace's house on that day. If I could direct your attention to page 3925 of the transcript, the colloquy the between colloquy myself and Mr. Jakovoski was the following: "Okay. Can you recall ..." -- Actually, I will start earlier than that, at line 1: "In 2001, where did the man known as Bucuk work, Bucuk? Answer: In the Kometa agency. Question: Okay. Can you recall the names of other persons who also worked or were associated with the Kometa agency in 2001? Answer: I cannot recall at that time. It was a long time ago. Question: Would you take a look at paragraph 24 again." This was paragraph 24 of the prior statement given by Mr. Jakovoski to the Office of the Prosecutor. It says: "Being asked who else I know from Kometa which were present in Ljuboten, I can name Bucuk Jovanovski; Johan Tarculovski; Sasa the one who was wounded; the brother of the wounded, Vlado Janevski, former department chief of the Kometa. These ones I can identify." Then I asked: "Does that help refresh your memory, inspector?" Mr. Jakovoski replied: "Yes. But I cannot remember now who this Vladko [sic] is and Sasa is. I have not seen them for seven years at least. Question: But at the time when you made this statement, this information was correct to the best of your knowledge? Answer: I cannot recall." Again, Your Honours, the only point that Mr. Jakovoski wanted to clarify was his lack of recollection regarding who Vlado Janevski and Sasa were; no attempt to clarify information related to the presence of Mr. Tarculovski. I'd like to turn the subject of Mr. Boskoski's knowledge of crimes committed at police stations and other cruel treatment locations. First of all, contrary to the submissions of my colleague yesterday, at page 11.075 of the transcript, the Prosecution's final brief makes submissions about Mr. Boskoski's effective control over police officers at police stations and other cruel treatment sites described in the indictment. I would refer the Chamber to paragraphs 269, 274 through 286, and 340 of the Prosecution's final brief. Your Honours, the only reasonable inference to be drawn from the evidence is that beginning in August 2001, after he established his sham investigative commission, Mr. Boskoski was, or at least should have been, aware that the police had subjected the detained residents from Ljuboten to cruel treatment at various police stations around Ljuboten. Risto Galevski, a member of the commission established by Minister Boskoski, was asked during his testimony whether the commission was aware of these allegations of cruel treatment in police stations in Skopje, or had them as part of their mandate. Mr. Galevski replied that he had insisted that his subordinates present him with such information, if indeed, they hadn't. This at page 3588 of the transcript. Mr. Galevski would not have made such a request unless he had reason and information to do so. Clearly, he was on notice that there may have been instances of cruel treatment in police stations around Ljuboten. The evidence of Mr. Galevski was that he and Goran Mitevski discussed the work of their commission on several occasions with Minister Boskoski. Furthermore, the information Mr. Boskoski had received prior to and immediately after the events in Ljuboten would have given him a heightened awareness of the likelihood that the detainees from Ljuboten might well be mistreated in custody. Exhibit P328 is a press release from Human Rights Watch, dated 31st of May, 2001. A press release that was widely distributed that reported on beatings and torture of ethnic Albanian detainees in police stations in Kumanovo and Skopje. Peter Bouckaert testified that this press release received extensive press coverage in Macedonia. Exhibit P361 is another widely circulated Human Rights Watch report, calling on the government of Macedonia to address violence against ethnic Albanians in police stations and citing a case of an ethnic Albanian beaten to death by the police on 13 August in the Beka 1 police station. This report from Human Rights Watch was issued on the 22nd of August, 2001. These reports gave Minister Boskoski notice of the likelihood of violence against the detainees from Ljuboten in the various police stations in which they were held. Furthermore, Exhibit P352, the Human Rights Watch report on the Ljuboten events, specifically referred to cruel treatment of detainees in Cair, Kisela Voda, and Karpos police stations. This would certainly have informed Minister Boskoski of the need to investigate the treatment of Ljuboten detainees in all the police stations in which they were held. Your Honours, my colleague's reliance yesterday on the Halilovic appeals judgement, at 11.077 to 11.078 of the transcript, and the von Leeb case, at 11.709, are also misplaced. These two cases deal with accused who lacked executive authority over the perpetrators of crimes. As I have mentioned already today, the circumstances of Mr. Boskoski in 2001, his degree of power, authority, and responsibility over the perpetrators of the crimes charged in this indictment were extensive. Mr. Mettraux referred you yesterday to the Kvocka judgement, page 11074 of the transcript, as support for his submission that Mr. Boskoski had no effective control over the perpetrators of the crimes. The important distinction, Your Honour, between Miroslav Kvocka at the Omarska death camp in Prijedor in 1992 and Mr. Boskoski in August 2001 was that Mr. Boskoski had the material ability to punish the perpetrators of the crimes. So the Kvocka judgement is also in opposite to these proceedings. At pages 11.077 to 11.078, my colleague focussed on the concepts of Mr. Boskoski's duties and obligations. The Prosecutor has made extensive submissions on this subject, at paragraphs 365 to 387 of its final brief. But it's important to recall two points: First, the Ministry of Internal Affairs made no genuine and competent efforts to investigate the crimes alleged in the indictment, to report the relevant facts to the judiciary and/or discipline the perpetrators. As the highest authority in the Ministry of Internal Affairs at the time, and the superior of the perpetrators the of these crime, Minister Boskoski had the duty and obligation to ensure that these activities occurred. I with refer you to Exhibits P86, the Law on Internal Affairs, and P88, particularly Articles 140 through 142, on this point. P88, as you know, is the Code of Criminal Procedure from Macedonia. Instead, Mr. Boskoski failed to even criticise the misconduct of the police that occurred between 10 -- excuse me, 12 and 14 of August 2001. Your Honours, I would also refer you to the testimony of Defence witness Petre Stojanovski, at pages 9270, 9093 to 9094, and 9371 to 9373. Petre Stojanovski described how one method used by the Macedonian police to learn about potential perpetrators of crimes was to speak with perpetrators of crimes, witnesses of crimes, and citizens. Petre Stojanovski also explained that the Macedonian police had an obligation to check out the facts, and "provide at least a minimum of relevant facts an information that could corroborate the notion that a crime had, indeed, been committed." Secondly, Your Honours, at page 11.081, my colleague submits that it was the Macedonian law that enabled Minister Boskoski to carry out his functions and which set limits on Mr. Boskoski's duties as minister. My colleague suggested that, once the duty officer from the Mirkovci police station notified the investigative judge on 12 August that there were dead bodies at Ljuboten, Mr. Boskoski's duties and obligations ceased. That would be a perverse interpretation of the law, indeed; and if correct, would create a huge gap in international humanitarian law. As the Prosecution submitted in its brief, the police only reported alleged acts of terrorism committed by ethnic Albanian residents of Ljuboten. The police never reported to the judiciary any facts about the crimes committed by the police between 12 and 14 August. Your Honours, if you take the Defence`s position to its extreme, that would mean that, hypothetically, a police unit could massacre an entire village of civilians, report to the judiciary merely that there were some persons killed in the village, and then the ministry of internal affairs could wash his hands of any additional responsibility for the matter. The Prosecution does not believe that international humanitarian law can be interrupted in this way. My colleagues mentioned yesterday a number of steps that Mr. Boskoski and the Ministry of Internal Affairs allegedly took to redress the crimes or investigate the crimes that occurred in and around Ljuboten and in and around Skopje. Your Honours, there is no credible evidence that steps were taken to genuinely investigate the cruel treatment of ethnic Albanian civilians at the Ametovski house, Brace's house, Buzalak check-point, the police stations referred to in the indictment, and the Basic Court in Skopje and Skopje City Hospital. I'd like to mention one of the steps referred to by my colleagues. It was a proposal for an exhumation that was submitted by Goran Mitevski, the director of the ministry's public security bureau, to the public prosecutor and the investigative judge that an exhumation be carried out at Ljuboten. This is Exhibit 1D33. If you take a look at the last paragraph of that document, you see that, for the Ministry of Internal Affairs and for the closest subordinate of Mr. Boskoski, the goal of the exhumation was to identify the five corpses and determine the cause of death of these five individuals. Nothing more. I would invite Your Honours to compare that document with Exhibit P55.02, under seal, the proposal of department public prosecutor, Dragoljub Cakic, that an exhumation be carried out. The public prosecutor wanted to address the real issue, the circumstances under which death occurred. The Ministry of Internal Affairs never advocated for that task to be carried out. My colleagues suggested yesterday that the Prosecution must prove that the accused's conduct, under Article 7(3), amounted to a "gross violation of his duties," and that the accused's breach of his duties must amount to acquiescence of toleration of the crimes. The Prosecution does not accept that this is the standard applied for Article 7(3) responsibility at this Tribunal. But even if it was, the evidence in this case meets that standard. Minister Boskoski's intention was not to redress the crimes that occurred between 10 and 14 August 2001. It was to tolerate them and to shield the perpetrators from accountability. My colleague yesterday suggested that Exhibit P464, the book entitled "The War in Macedonia" should be given little weight, allegedly because it is uncorroborated by other evidence; but the record of this trial tells us otherwise. For example, P464 refers to the existence of a war in Macedonia during 2001. That evidence is corroborated by Peter Bouckaert, at page 3242 of the transcript. Information in "The War in Macedonia" about the goals and objectives of the NLA were corroborated by Nazim Bushi; pages 6043 to 6046 of the transcript. Exhibit P493, page 3, corroborates "The War in Macedonia" description of the NLA and its abilities during 2001. My colleagues told you yesterday that the evidence of M-084, about the issuance of radios and bullet-proof vests at OVR Cair on the 11th of August, is uncorroborated. But that's not correct. Witness M-052 referred to the fact that a number of the members of the police unit that followed Mr. Tarculovski into the village that day had bullet-proof vests. Witness M-037 described the fact that Mr. Tarculovski had a two-way radio with him in Ljuboten on the 12th of August. My colleagues told you yesterday that the unit for professional standards in the Ministry of Internal Affairs was not operating in 2001, but that submission is belied by Exhibit P00395, the 92 bis statement of Kire Rusevski, who explains that the unit for professional standards was very much operating in 2001, although it was expanded during 2002. I'd like to turn my attention now to the comments of my colleague Mr. Apostolski, with respect to the accused Johan Tarculovski. First of all, Your Honours, the Prosecution has never argued that a joint criminal enterprise extended beyond 12 August 2001. It has always been the Prosecution's position that "the joint criminal enterprise came into existence no earlier than Friday, 10 August 2001, and continued up to and including Sunday, 12 August 2001." That's at paragraph 4 of the Second Amended Indictment. At paragraph 59 of the Prosecution's amended pre-trial brief, the Prosecution explains that the common plan of the joint criminal enterprise "would have had to be in place before the police entered the village, or, at the very least, developed extremely rapidly after the first crimes were committed." However, evidence of a cover-up after the 12th of August can constitute evidence of the common purpose of the joint criminal enterprise within the time-period of 10 to 12 August, and I would refer the Chamber to the Krajisnik trial judgement, paragraphs 970 and 1.054 on this point. The Defence for Mr. Boskoski and Mr. Tarculovski submit that the Prosecution has failed to prove that persons with criminal backgrounds participated in the Ljuboten events. This at pages 11.108 and 11.136 of yesterday's transcript. The evidence on this point is set out fully in paragraphs 43 and 44 of the Prosecution's final brief. The evidence of witnesses, such as M-052 and M-084, along with M-053, Exhibits P591, 1D326, P231, under seal, demonstrate that persons who received weapons at OVR Cair on 11 August had criminal records and that such persons participated in the Ljuboten operation. These criminal records are set out in Exhibit P592. By the way, I should have mentioned a moment ago, also P232, under seal. With respect to one of these persons, Ilija Sekarovski, his criminal record is also set out in Exhibit P231 at ERN N006-4710. As to the persons listed in Exhibit P232, M-084 recognised at least one of those persons who did not have a clean record. This is at page 1.475 of the transcript. My colleague suggested yesterday that the criminal records for these persons were expunged; but if these records were expunged, Your Honours, then how was it possible to determine what these records are and what they say, as Exhibit P592 demonstrates. The Defence claim that persons -- that the persons who have criminal records indicated in Exhibit P592, as shown to witness Popovski, became police reservists as of the 16th of August, 2001. But, on the contrary, the evidence that you've heard proves that these persons came to OVR Cair on the 10th and 11th of August to be issued weapons. They were given police uniforms and they became reservists, or they wore police uniforms and they became reservists. At page 11.115 of the transcript, my colleague Mr. Apostolski appeared to argue that the Prosecution has been inconsistent by relying on Exhibit 487, a map produced by Gzim Ostreni, to describe places that you were under the control of the NLA, and, at the same time, keeping its position that the NLA were not present in Ljuboten on the 12th of August. Your Honours, these two positions are not mutually exclusive. The evidence of Henry Bolton, at page 1.608 of the transcript, described how the concept of control over territory can mean areas where Macedonian government authorities were unable to function in 2001. Control does not necessarily equal presence. As an example, Your Honour, while the United States military may be said to have been in control of South Vietnam during parts of the 1960s and 1970s, that does not mean that the United States military had a physical presence in every South Vietnamese village. The same principle can apply to Exhibit P487 and the village of Ljuboten, and as Nazim Bushi described at page 5605 of the transcript: "The village of Ljuboten was within the zone of responsibility of the NLA's 114th Brigade, but not within its area of operation." Your Honours, there has been no change to the Prosecution's case theory. At pages 11.115 to 11.116, Mr. Apostolski argued that the Prosecution has attempted to change the theory of its case because it makes submissions in its final brief about the possibility that the victims at Ljuboten were hors de combat. Your Honours, the indictment in paragraphs 23, Count 1, and 42, Count 3, refers to Article 3(1)(a) of the Geneva Conventions; namely, a provision of common Article 3 to the Geneva Conventions which refers to persons hors de combat. And in addition, paragraph 117 of the Prosecution's pre-trial brief specifically refers to persons hors de combat. It says: "There is an additional general requirement, under common Article 3, that victims be mere bystanders to the hostilities, including civilians, members of the armed forces who have laid down their arms and those placed hors de combat." Yesterday, at page 11.117, Mr. Apostolski acknowledged that there were over 2.000 civilians in the village of Ljuboten on the weekend of 10 to 12 August. That fact was enough to make any participant in the Ljuboten attack aware of the likelihood that any ethnic Albanian who they encountered on 12 August was a civilian, but that awareness did not temper the behaviour of the police units that entered Ljuboten on 12 August. At page 11.118, Mr. Apostolski argued that the attack on Ljuboten targeted only members of the NLA who were allegedly present in Ljuboten village and that no common plan to target civilians ever existed. Your Honours, the evidence about the presence of the NLA in Ljuboten taking at its highest in support of the Defence position demonstrates that, at most, there were three armed NLA members in the village, because only three weapons, those allegedly found near the Jashari house, were recovered from Ljuboten on 12 August. Why, then, were the persons at the Ametovski house also targeted? Why were they beaten and killed? Why was Rami Jusufi killed? Why were so many houses burned? Your Honours, the Prosecution agrees with the position of the Tarculovski Defence, expressed yesterday at page 11.121 of the transcript that "no civilian was killed in the cross-fire." No civilians were killed by cross-fire on the 12th of August because the members of the Macedonian police deliberately shot to death the persons who died at Ljuboten: Sulejman Bajrami, Muharem Ramadani, Xhelal Bajrami, Bajram Jashari, and Kadri Jashari. The explanation given by my learned colleague that no civilian was killed in the cross-fire due to the precautions of the security forces is a puzzling interpretation of the evidence, to say the least. Your Honours, the evidence admitted in this trial does not demonstrate that President Trajkovski issued an order for the security forces to carry out the Ljuboten attack on the 12th of August. The evidence demonstrates that the only possible instruction given by the president was his comment to Major Despodov to undertake measures and activities that were within his competence so that the operation at Ljuboten was successful. You find this at Mitre Despodov's testimony at pages 2579 to 2580, and Mr. Keskovski's testimony at page 10.139. Exhibit P304 contains a phrase suggesting that President Trajkovski ordered that the attack on Ljuboten should begin on the morning of 11 August; but if the president issued such an order, it was not obeyed. The president was certainly unaware of the attack on Ljuboten on 12 August, as evidenced by the testimony of Defence witness Keskovski, who described how, on the morning of 12 August, the president received information "that something was happening with the civilian population that had gathered in the village of Radisani." Nothing more. Page 10.112 of the transcript. After the events of 12 August, President Trajkovski asked Mr. Tarculovski if he had been in Ljuboten. This is at pages 10.028 to 10.029, and 10.019 to 10.120 of the transcript. If President Trajkovski had commanded the Ljuboten operation, as the Defence suggest, it is highly unlikely that the president would have asked such a question to Mr. Tarculovski, the leader of the police unit that attacked Ljuboten. Finally, even if you accept the Defence position that the president gave certain orders pertaining to the Ljuboten attack, there is no evidence that the president's orders somehow erased the effective control, including the material ability to punish, that Mr. Boskoski exercised over the police officers who carried out the attack. At page 11.112 of the transcript, (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: (redacted) Mitre Despodov "would also be in charge of taking other measures." There was no mention of any order from President Trajkovski. Indeed, there was no mention of President Trajkovski at all. This is at page 8.270 to 8.271 and pages 8.312 to 8.313. Your Honours, at page 11.126 of the transcript yesterday, just a few minutes after relying on the testimony of M-052, (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: (redacted), Mr. Apostolski urged you to disregard the evidence of M-052 in its entirety, alleging that M-052's evidence is false, unreliable, and self-serving. That is a puzzling argument, indeed, given that the Tarculovski Defence seeks to rely on important parts of M-052's testimony. At page 11.130, (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: At page 11.124 of yesterday's transcript, my colleague told the Chamber: "After the resistance was neutralized, the attack stopped." Your Honours, leaving aside the shooting of three men at the Jashari house, just what was "neutralized" at the Ametovski house? The evidence shows that men and women there were forced to leave the basements where they had taken shelter, and the men were cruelly beaten and then the police shot two of them. The attack on civilians at Ljuboten did not stop until the ten men detained at the Ametovski house were put on a truck bound for the Mirkovci police station, where the cruel treatment continued. At page 11.142, Mr. Apostolski argues that the attack on Ljuboten was a legitimate anti-terrorist operation and that there was no plan to attack civilians during that attack. Your Honours, at that time, in addition to the new Lions unit, the Ministry of Internal Affairs had, at a minimum, the posebna unit and the Tigers special police unit. If this was a legitimate anti-terrorist operation, the Ministry of Internal Affairs would have used one of those units in the attack on Ljuboten. We know from the evidence of Mr. Galevski and others that the posebna was available on the 12th of August, 2001. Mr. Tarculovski, as a regular member of the Ministry of Internal Affairs and part of its security sector, would have been aware of the existence of these special police units trained for legitimate operations. Mr. Boskoski, during his time at Brace's house on the 12th of August, might also have asked himself why neither the posebna unit nor the Tigers unit were present. Your Honours, if this was a legitimate anti-terrorist operation, why were persons with criminal records used to execute the operation? If that was a legitimate anti-terrorist operation, why were volunteer police reservists, individuals with the least amount of police training, used to carry out the operation? And if that was a legitimate anti-terrorist operation, Your Honours, why did the police officers burn crosses in the back of detained persons, beat them, and kill them? At page 11.127 of the transcript, my colleague argued that, in general, that Mr. Tarculovski was not in control of the situation at Ljuboten and had no authority over the other police officers who entered the village that day. But the evidence is overwhelming that Mr. Tarculovski was the leader of the police unit that attacked Ljuboten with authority over the participants in the attack. On the 10th and 11th of August, Mr. Tarculovski procured assistance for the police unit. On the evening of 11 August, Mr. Tarculovski told Major Despodov: "Tomorrow, I will start the action." That's in Exhibit P302 and P303. On the 12th of August, (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: (redacted) further into the village because artillery support from the army units was expected. It was Mr. Tarculovski who explained the situation to M-037 at the Ametovski house, and it was Mr. Tarculovski who told M-037 that an inspection was not necessary at the Jashari house. At page 11.128, Mr. Apostolski argues that the Prosecution failed to prove that Mr. Tarculovski made his comment, "There is no need for an inspection. This is a state of war," from a position of authority. But this is circular reasoning, indeed, since Mr. Tarculovski's comment proved his position of authority. M-052 described the role of Mr. Tarculovski this way, at page 8271: "These units that was -- that came, responsible for that unit was Mr. Johan. He was their boss. Whether he had a rank or not, I don't know. I didn't know what was his position. I know only that he was their boss." Mr. Apostolski argued that the Prosecution checked the records at Basic Court I in Skopje, the records of the public prosecutor, and the Ministry of Internal Affairs, and yet was unable to identify the individual perpetrators of the crimes alleged in the indictment. Well, that's correct, and that's because Mr. Boskoski and his subordinates failed to carry out their duties in 2001. Mr. Apostolski argued that Mr. Tarculovski knew that the three individuals killed near the Jashari house were not civilians because they were armed; therefore, Your Honours, Mr. Tarculovski and his colleagues must have known that the persons they detained at the Ametovski house were civilians because they were not armed. Mr. Apostolski argued that the presence of civilians will not render a target immune from attack. This is at page 11.120 of yesterday's transcript. But the Prosecution would respectfully refer Your Honours to the Galic appeals judgement, at paragraph 194, referring to the Galic trial judgement at paragraph 61, where the Appeals Chamber noted that the failure of a party to abide by its obligations under international humanitarian law does not relieve the attacking side of its duty to abide by the principles of distinction and proportionality when launching an attack. Your Honours, the evidence proves that on 12 August 2001, the police unit that attacked the village of Ljuboten cast the principle of distinction to the winds, and that is why we are present before you today, and the Prosecution asks that you find both accused guilty of the crimes charged in the indictment. Those are the submissions that I intended to make, Your Honours. I don't know if you have any questions for me. If not, I will sit down.

utterances.text: I take it you anticipate your submissions and those of Mr. Tarculovski finishing well within the appointed time? Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
