utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, good morning, Mr. President. We'll start with responding to some of the arguments which were made yesterday by the Office of the Prosecutor, and we'll deal with the issues raised anew today after the break, Your Honour. The first issue we would like to respond to is a submission made by the Prosecution in response to the Defence submission of a so-called village story, a version of the event which, in part, was agreed upon by the villagers and repeated in this courtroom. In response to the Defence submissions on that point, Prosecution has invited the Chamber to ignore a clear pattern of evidential tailoring, and are suggesting, at page 10.092 of the transcript: "The evidence of the crime-base witnesses has remained consistent and unchanged in relation to important issues." In particular, the Prosecution said the following: "The crime-base witnesses have remained steadfast in their identification of the perpetrators of these crimes. They were either uniformed police officers, or, in some of the cases of cruel treatment, civilians acting with the permission and encouragement of the police." The suggestion that the villagers, Your Honour, were steadfast in that regard is incorrect, and the suggestion that the Chamber could rely on the consistency, so-called, of the testimony in trial in that regard as proof of its reliability is unwarranted. Your Honours, at the time when some of the villagers were interviewed by the authorities, the Macedonian judicial authorities, and I refer in particular to P47, out of the 16 persons who had been interviewed, only one of them suggested to have been the witness to any incident of mistreatment at check-points. A number of the witnesses referred to incident of attempted mistreatment by civilians. This evidence, Your Honour, or this information has disappeared from the story told in this courtroom. Concerning the same 16 persons, again in P47, and concerning the police stations, which does not include Mirkovci police, there is only one person who alleged a mistreatment and does not identify whether that person was or wasn't a member of the police. The fact that their story has now changed and that they are now all claiming that it was police officers that mistreated them and that none of them mentioned incidents of mistreatment at the hands of civilians does not show reliability, Your Honour. Quite to the contrary, it shows and confirms the Defence submissions that some of the witnesses have agreed to recite a particular version in this courtroom. A second issue, Your Honour, which we would like to address briefly is that of effective control. At page 11.014, after making submissions about the alleged relevance of certain documents, the Prosecution took the following view: "All of this evidence, Your Honour, is further proof of the effective control that Mr. Boskoski exercised over members of the Minister of Internal Affairs and the police." That statement, Your Honour, not only gravely misunderstand whom the requirement of effective control refers to, but it is also indicative of the fact that, as submitted by the Defence yesterday, the Prosecution is just trying to prove the wrong fact. For the purpose of international law, Your Honours, the relationship of effective control that must be shown to exist in relation to the accused is one with the perpetrators and not, as the Prosecutor has sought to assert, with the police or the members of the ministry generally. I can refer, for instance, to Aleksovski Appeals Chamber, paragraph 76; Blaskic Appeals Chamber, 67; Stakic Trial Chamber, 459; Celebici Appeals Chamber, 249 and 992; among others. As we noted in our final brief, Your Honour, and repeated yesterday in our closing argument, the Prosecution is just trying to prove the wrong fact and, effectively, relies upon the theory of overall command that the Appeals Chamber in Halilovic has expressly rejected. I would wish, Your Honour, to take a minute in this courtroom to cite from the High Command case, the case from the Second World War, at page 543 to 544, which may be relevant to your considerations. The military Tribunal said this: "Military subordination is a comprehensive but not conclusive factor in fixing criminal responsibility. The authority, both administrative and military, of a commander and his criminal responsibility are related but by no means co-extensive. A high commander cannot keep completely informed of the details of military operations of subordinate and, most assuredly, not of every administrative measure. He has the right to assume that details entrusted to responsible subordinates will be legally executed. "The President of the United States is Commander in Chief of its military forces. Criminal acts committed by those forces cannot in themselves be charged to him on the theory of subordination. The same is true," the Tribunal continued, "of other higher commanders in the chain of command. Criminality does not attach to every individual in this chain of command from that fact alone. There must be a personal dereliction that can occur only where the act is directly traceable to believe him or where his failure to properly supervise his subordinate constitute criminal negligence on his part. "In the later case, it must be a personal neglect amounting to a wanton, immoral disregard of the action of his subordinates amounting to acquiescence. Any other interpretation of international law," the Tribunal concludes, "would go far beyond the basic principles of criminal law as known to civilized nations." Your Honour, another matter pertaining to the effective control case of the Prosecution concern the police stations. We have asserted yesterday in our closing argument that the Prosecution had effectively abandoned its effective control case in relation to the police station, the court, and the hospital. Mr. Saxon, in response, has cited to a number of paragraphs in the Prosecution final brief, suggesting that those paragraph, in fact, contain the submissions of the Prosecution in that regard. We invite the Chamber to look at those paragraph and to ascertain whether any basis as would allow the Chamber to make a finding of effective control is to be found in those paragraphs. Your Honour, we submit that none is present, and we invite the Chamber, again, to consider that part of the Prosecution case as having been abandoned. Your Honours, the Prosecution is also claiming that the law, Macedonian law, was more than bent a little in the Ministry of Interior at the time, and that situation could come to legal life without all the necessary requirements having been met. In our submissions, Your Honour, this proposition is not only artificial but it is not supported in evidence. The Prosecution is apparently trying to suggest that because some situation could be established without the strict requirements of the law having been met, it is open and reasonable to this Chamber to conclude that this was the case with the people who entered Ljuboten on the 12th of August. In other words, despite the absence of any evidence that these people had met the strict legal requirements of the law, you are invited to regard them as reservists anyway. There are many problems with that proposition and such an inference is not open. First, proof of the existence of a relationship of superior to subordinate, as is relevant to the law of command responsibility, must be proved beyond a reasonable doubt. To the extent that the case of the Prosecution is now one to be made by inference, Your Honour, this inference would have to be the only one available, the only reasonable inference open on the evidence. The standard would not be made in the present case, where the Defence has put on the record that many of those alleged by the Prosecution to have been in Ljuboten were not, in fact, members or officials of the ministry. Furthermore, and insofar as the Prosecution argument depends on proof having been made that it was possible for a person to become a reservist of the police without fulfilling the conditions of the law, proof of that fact has not been made. There is not one single example on the record of a reservist or of a person having become a reservist without the requirement of the law having been met. The Prosecution is effectively asking you not to draw an inference but to disregard the law and the evidence in favour of a fact that it cannot prove. In effect, you are asked to make the following or to follow the following reasoning, Your Honour: Despite the clear requirements of the law to the contrary, you are asked to come to the view that the person may be become a reservist without fulfilling those legal requirements, and you should, therefore, set aside and disregard both the law and the fact that no example of this ever happened. Then you are asked to assume that this is what happened in Ljuboten, again without any evidence of that fact, and also despite evidence to the contrary, Your Honour. You are further invited to take the view that this was the case in particular in relation to the perpetrators, again a fact that the Prosecution has failed to prove. I will remind the Chamber, once again, that not a single one of the alleged perpetrators has been identified. Your Honours, with all due respect, this is not an inference that is sought of you, that is pure fiction; and the allegation of the Prosecution on that point is not just deficient factually or evidently, but it is also contrary to its own pleadings. At page 11.016, the Prosecution argues that the de jure requirements should not be determinative of Mr. Boskoski's effective control over those police officers. But the fact is, Your Honour, that the sole basis of the alleged relationship between Mr. Boskoski and the alleged perpetrators is the fact that Mr. Boskoski was the minister of the interior at the time. That position, as well as the duties and relationships of the ministers, are regulated by law and no where else. There is nothing de facto about the position of the minister of the interior in Macedonia, nor is there anything de facto about being a reservist, Your Honour. The concept of a de facto reservist simply does not exist. So when the Prosecution claims that the determinative factor is a material ability to punish crimes, not a legal authority to do so, he is not just legally incorrect as regard the charges against Mr. Boskoski, and as explained yesterday, but he also goes against the pleadings according to which the duties and obligation of Mr. Boskoski are founded in law in Macedonia and which allegedly linked him to the alleged perpetrators. Your Honour, simply for the record, we would also indicate that the theory of the Prosecution, whereby individuals could have become members or reservists of the Ministry of Interior without fulfilling the requirements of the law, is contrary to the evidence of many witnesses who testified in this courtroom. And as pointed out by my colleague Mr. Apostolski in his closing yesterday, unless the Prosecution is willing to confront that evidence, it may not seek from the Chamber an inference to the contrary. I will simply refer to the transcript at page 5.111, 4.909, 9.115, to 9.116, 6.827 to 6.828, 1.971, 4.918, 3.717 to 3.722, and also page 10.671 to 10.672, an Exhibit 1D310, paragraph 47. All of this evidence, Your Honour, is in plain contradiction with the Prosecution's theory and remains unchallenged. Would that be a convenient time, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Mr. Mettraux. We adjourn now and will resume after the normal break at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Mettraux.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'd like to move on briefly, Your Honours, to the issue of the alleged armed conflict and the alleged mens rea relevant to that conflict. The Prosecution, Your Honours, we note has not addressed an important issue that we pointed out to in our brief; namely, the status of the actions of the NLA as terrorist activities and the consequence which this may have on the Prosecution ability to establish an armed conflict. We won't reiterate here our submissions here on that point, and simply refer to our final brief. There is, however, a related issue that we would like to highlight, and simply to point out that, as indicated in our brief, acts of terrorism do not constitute evidence of the existence of an armed conflict and fall outside the realm of international humanitarian law. As mentioned in the UK Manual on the Laws of War, which we cite in our briefs at paragraphs 265, acts of terrorism do not amount to an armed conflict. This means that to establish the existence of an armed conflict, Your Honour, the Prosecution could not rely on those incidents which amount to terrorist activities. This issue, Your Honours, is relevant not just to whether or not there was an armed conflict at the time in the former Yugoslavia Republic of Macedonia, but also whether to the related question of whether it was reasonable for Mr. Boskoski to take the view that the situation was not an armed conflict. Here, Your Honour, the important fact is that at all times Mr. Boskoski and the Ministry of Interior regarded and described the activities and attacks of the NLA as example in cases of terrorist activities. I will refer, Your Honour, in particular, as a matter of example, to Exhibit 1D342, which lists a number of incidents which the Prosecution claims are relevant to establishing the intensity, so they say, of the armed conflict, but which, in fact, are regarded as instances of terrorism. And when my colleagues, Your Honours, said that what matters is the accused awareness of the relevant factual circumstances on which to judge finally whether the existence of an armed conflict internal in this case was established, she was quite right. What was incorrect, however, Your Honour, is to suggest that the facts to which the Prosecution pointed to would have been relevant to establishing such a state of mind. In effect, the Prosecution is pointing to a number of factual incidents, acts of terrorism, as evidence, they say, of Mr. Boskoski's mens rea. In effect, the Prosecution has only established that Mr. Boskoski knew of incidents which are irrelevant to establishing the existing -- the existence of an armed conflict. In other words, the Prosecution has failed to establish that he was aware of the factual basis that would have made it possible for him to come to that view. In other words, the Prosecution failed to establish the mens rea relevant to Article 3 of the Statute. Counsel for the Prosecution has responded to Defence submissions as regards possible mistake of law and mistake of fact by suggesting that it is not for the Prosecution to exclude the possibility of such a mistake. Your Honour, this is quite wrong. First, concerning the technical issue of the burden of proof, it is clear that the burden is upon the Prosecution at all times. It is for the Prosecution to exclude the reasonable possibility that the accused might have committed an excusable mistake of fact or an excusable mistake of law which might offer him a full defence to the charges. As authority for that proposition, Your Honour, I will cite, in particular, a case Michael A. Schwartz, which is a US Court Marshall judgement of 21st June 1970. It's an appeal decision at page 862 to 864. The Prosecution is equally incorrect when it is dismissing this defence, or at least the submissions pertaining to this defence, as unimportant in this context. The Defence in particular, and the Defence of mistake of law more specifically, plays a significant part and a significant role under international criminal law insofar as it compensates, in part, for the general lack of precision of that body. The judge advocate in the Peleus case, again a case from the Second World War, said this: "No sailor and no soldier can carry with him a library of international law." This is equally true of civilian leaders, Your Honour. And as a result of the law's uncertainty, and as pointed out by Professor Cassese, the first president of this Tribunal, he said this: "As a countervailing factor to these flaws of international criminal law, court therefore tend to attach to mistake of law a greater weight than the one most national legal systems attribute to the same excuse." And as a matter of illustration, Your Honour, of that principle, I can cite, for instance, to the hostage case, where the following said: "Where room exists for an honest error in judgement, such army commander is entitled to the benefit thereof by virtue of the presumption of innocence." This principle, or these defences of mistake of law and mistakes of facts, are relevant, Your Honour, in our submissions, not just to the question of whether or not there was an armed conflict and whether or not it was reasonable for Mr. Boskoski to take the view that there wasn't, but also, as we indicated in our submission, to the issue of whether or not he would have been entitled to come to the conclusion that he had fulfilled all those duties that the law relevant to these proceedings required of him. I will cite again, this time not verbatim, from a different case where the principle stated is as follows: Where the accused believed in good faith that he was entitled to act as he did or that his conduct was in conformity with his obligation, he may be said to have been mistaken about the unlawfulness and criminal character of his conduct if, indeed, that conduct is shown to have been otherwise criminal and may not be held criminally reliable. This case, Your Honour, is In Re B; it's a Dutch case from the Field Court Marshall, a decision of the 2nd of January, 1951, which is reported in "The Netherlands 1952" at page 247. The Prosecution today, Your Honour, in its brief has reiterated the suggestion that Mr. Boskoski and Mr. Tarculovski were present together at Brace's house. As we have indicated in our brief, and in our submissions, the evidence does not support such a case. The Prosecution relies upon the evidence of two persons, M-037 and Mr. Jakovoski. Starting with M-037, Your Honour, the Prosecution has cited to pages of the transcript where Mr. Saxon, indeed, read back to the witness a statement which that witness had given earlier. The content or that part of the statement upon which the Prosecution now seeks to rely was never put to the witness. The witness never adopted that part of the statements upon which the Prosecution seeks to rely. To the extent that this is evidence, Your Honour, this is the evidence of counsel, not of the witness. M-037 never claimed in evidence before this trial that he saw Mr. Tarculovski and Mr. Boskoski together. If that was the Prosecution's case, it should have put it to the witness. And, Your Honours, I draw your attention to page 875 and 876, which counsel has read to you, in part. Following the part that was read to you by the Prosecution, the Prosecution said this: "All right. Thank you. That is all I want to deal with this document." Mr. Saxon said: "I don't need to deal with anything else in this document. Can that document then now be removed, please." Your Honour, it is our submissions that on a matter of such importance and to the extent that the Prosecution intended to elicit such evidence from this witness, it had the duty to put the proposition in question to the witness. It failed to do so. Concerning the second witness on which the Prosecution seeks to rely, Mr. Jakovoski, the situation is very similar. Mr. Jakovoski never adopted the content of the statement that counsel read to him. In fact, he positively rejected it when asked specifically by counsel. In that regard, I can cite, in particular, from page 2935, where the following page was asked of him: "Can you recall seeing Minister Boskoski and Bucuk and Johan Tarculovski together during the crisis time in 2001?" The answer was: "I cannot recall this either." Elsewhere in the transcript, Your Honour, the same witness, Mr. Jakovoski, indicated that he did not even know what Mr. Tarculovski looks like. It is page 3942. Therefore, to the extent that the Prosecution suggests that Mr. Jakovoski gave positive evidence of a sighting of Mr. Boskoski and Mr. Tarculovski together, the record does not support such a proposition. Today, Your Honour, the Prosecution has also taken issue with submissions made by counsel in the course of yesterday's closing argument, concerning the degree of fault necessary to entail superior responsibility under international criminal law. The Defence has indicated that the standard to be met was that of a gross breach of duty which amounted, effectively, to acquiescence on the part of the superior. The Prosecution has indicated that this was not law the of this Tribunal and that there was no support support for the Defence proposition on that point. First, I would like to cite from the Bagilishema, the Appeals Chamber judgement of the ICTR Tribunal. Paragraph 36, the Appeals Chamber said this: "Depending upon the nature of the breach of duty, "and that refers to the duties of a superior, "which must be a gross breach, and the gravity the consequence thereof breaches of duties imposed by the laws of war maintain a disciplinary rather than a criminal liability of a superior who is subject to military discipline. So what the Appeals Chamber said is that it was, in fact, a requirement of international law that the duty -- the breach of duty be gross in nature. Secondly, and insofar as relevant to the law of superior responsibility which is applied in this Tribunal as is indicated, inter alia, in the Hadzihasanovic Appeals Chamber judgement of this Tribunal, this is customary international law which rules. Therefore, the cases to which the Defence has referred in page 15 to 20 of tab 25 of your binder are foundational precedents of international criminal law, an extremely important indication of the state of international law on that point; and all of them, Your Honour, we submit, support the point of the Defence. The Prosecution has not explained why or how this Chamber could disregard this standard. As an additional matter, we will simply draw Your Honours' attention to the position of the ICRC on that point, which said this at paragraph 3451 of its commentary to additional Protocol I. It says that: "To be criminal, the dereliction that is to be attributed to a commander or a superior must be so serious that it is tantamount to malicious intent apart from any link between the conduct in question and the damage that took place." In various cases that took place after the Second World War, the standard which was regarded by this Tribunal as relevant to liability for this form of responsibility was that of acquiescence. Perhaps, I will read briefly, again, the conclusion of the High Command case in relation to this matter, where it said that: "The dereliction must be personal neglect amounting to a wanton, immoral disregard of the action of his subordinates amounting to acquiescence. Any other interpretation of international law would go far beyond the basic principles of criminal law as known to civilized nations." Your Honour, I'm grateful for your patience, and now I give the floor to Ms. Residovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mettraux. Ms. Residovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. In the course of today's rebuttal, the Prosecutor touched on the Defence position that the Ministry of Interior, when informing the investigating judge, had carried out its duty, and commented on this by saying that such an interpretation of the position of the minister of the interior would amount to a serious violation of international law. Your Honours, the Macedonian state has ordered an entire system of detecting and prosecuting perpetrators of crimes. In this system, as you have seen from the evidence admitted and from the testimony of the witnesses heard here, particular organs have certain duties and responsibilities. As has been shown in the evidence presented, at the point of time when the duties of one body or organ cease, the duties are taken up by another organ. So, in the Republic of Macedonia, there is no possibility for orders to detect and prosecute crimes. It cannot fail to be carried out in full. You have heard testimonies to this effect, as I have already said: Vilma Ruskovska, the deputy prosecutor, and also the testimony of Petre Stojanovski. Therefore, at no point is there any vacuum or gap where someone might wash his hands of a crime they had committed. The only issue is who had the legal duty and responsibility to act and in what direction was that action taken. The Prosecutor used only one example, saying that that would be the action taken by the police, and this is the information of the 12th of August that there were corpses in the villages. However, our written submissions and the evidence in the case shows that neither on the 12th nor on the 14th did the ministry cease cooperating actively with the other judicial organs in order to throw light on the events in Ljuboten and the surrounding area. Your Honours, we have provided evidence to support this, and this evidence has been dealt with in full in our written submissions. So I will not repeat them now. The Prosecutor, however, wishes to show that the Ministry of Interior didn't really want to investigate the events and gave an example; that is, Exhibit 1D33. This is the proposal for exhumation and post-mortem which was submitted on the 7th of September to the public prosecutor's office and the duty investigating judge of the Basic Court in Skopje by the ministry. Referring to this exhibit, the Prosecutor claims without foundation that this exhibit goes to show that the ministry did not have the intention of throwing light on the events and establishing all the relevant facts and circumstances. Your Honours, I will take the liberty of reading the closing sentence of this proposal, in which the Ministry of Interior explains its proposal by saying that the identity of five corpses must be established, as well as the cause of death from the five individuals from Ljuboten village. To establish the reason or the cause of death means establishing all circumstances and reasons and the conditions due to which the death of the aforementioned individuals occurred. In relation to this proposal, you have heard witnesses, Vilma Ruskovska and others, that this exhumation request was actually an initiative that went beyond the responsibilities and the competences of the minister of the interior towards the justice system bodies. This business after the knowledge that the bodies were buried was in the hands of the prosecutor himself. But since the prosecutor did not do that within the next 20 days, it was the ministry who initiated the aforementioned procedure, precisely due to the reasons that the Defence indicated, because it was important for the minister and for the ministry to clarify and elucidate all events and to justly and properly establish all facts and circumstances. The best illustration that this is correct is the information compiled by the commission established by Mr. Boskoski on the 13th of August, which states at the end of its opinion: "In order to analyse the issue at stake and have a comprehensive approach, it is necessary that the competent structures in the Republic of Macedonia undertake legitimate action, exhumation of the corpses in the presence of experts, as well as representatives of the interested international organisations which would have as its consequence undertaking of all necessary legal measures, in order to ascertain all relevant facts and obtain the answer to the open and essential issue for this case." So it is precisely the opposite of the position of the Prosecutor that the ministry was unwilling to learn about the circumstances of the case. The documents that were received in evidence, Your Honours, testify to the opposite. And, finally, in relation to this issue raised by my learned colleague the Prosecutor today, I wish to refer to Exhibit 1D73; that is, the Official Note that speaks to the meeting which took place on the 14th of September, 2002 [as interpreted] in the Forensic Medicine Institute -- 2001, upon the initiative of the investigating judge, Nikolovski, which from the very beginning, acting upon the proposal of the public prosecutor and upon the initiative of the Ministry of Interior, was in charge of the Ljuboten case from the beginning until the end, until it was deferred to the competence of the international Tribunal. This document reads: "In the meeting, the investigating judge, Nikolovski, informed the attendants that the Ministry of Interior has submitted to the basic public prosecutor's office, Skopje, an information note on the activities undertaken in the area of Ljuboten by the security forces of the Ministry of Interior." So, Your Honours, it is exactly the opposite from what the Prosecutor suggests. The evidence in this case show all due responsible of the ministry and the Minister Boskoski in performing all duty that they had under the law but to go even beyond, to ascertain all facts related to the events and any liability, if there would be evidence that would lead to reasonable suspicion. So, this is a direction according to which I am referencing also Exhibit P88, Article 42, which clearly speaks about the duties of the public prosecutor within the criminal procedure, who has the task of being in charge of the pre-trial procedure. That is the stage when the crimes are detected. Article 144, paragraph 2 of that same law, P88, which clearly stipulates that at the moment when the public prosecutor obtains knowledge that there is an reason to suspect that a crime has been committed, that he is then dominus litis who puts requests to other organs, so also to the Ministry of Interior which are the tasks that they need to undertake. So all the other evidence that you have on record absolutely deny the allegations of my learned colleague. In his closing arguments, the Prosecutor, attempting to demonstrate the de facto control of the minister of the interior over the police, refers, inter alia, to the fact that the minister in 2001 issued an order to interrupt annual leaves and the testimony of Miodrag Stojanovski who said that this order reached the police stations. Your Honours, not for a single moment did the Defence claim that a minister cannot issue an order. The Defence, however, has stated clearly, and the evidence points to this, that the minister could issue an order when authorised to do so by the law. We have mentioned more than once Exhibit P92, Article 55. This is the Law on the Organisation of the State Administration which enumerates the authorities and the powers of the minister, if he is empowered to implement them by the law. As for the specific issues raised by my learned friend when referring to the de facto control of Mr. Boskoski, when he issued an order to interrupt annual leave, this right of his is founded directly on the law and is one of the exceptional cases when a minister may issue an order. This can be seen in Exhibit P86, Article 61, which says the following: "When the needs of the ministry so require, the minister, or an officer authorised by them, could delay or terminate the annual vacation of an employee." So it is the opposite from the assertion of the Prosecutor. This example, again, corroborates the position of the Defence that the minister had certain rights, when explicitly provided with them by the law, to also issue certain decisions. In a part of his closing arguments where the Prosecutor wishes to show that there was some situations which existed de facto before they came into being de jure, the Prosecutor refers, inter alia, to the testimony of witness M-056, claiming that this witness held the position of senior inspector, although the post did not exist in legal terms at the time. With respect to the same circumstance, Your Honours, we heard the testimony of General Zoran Jovanovski, who stated clearly, when this question was put to him, that Exhibit 1D62, from which the Prosecutor deduced that the status of senior inspector existed before it was regulated by law, the witness said that this rule book on the modification and amendments, in fact, only amended the rules in item 5 by introducing into 5.1 the battalion called Lavovi, Lions, Rapid Intervention Battalion which was established under exhibit -- from the testimony of M-056. That's on transcript pages 49 -- I apologise. I will give you pages later. As well as from the exhibits, it follows quite clearly that the title, "senior advisor," existed before, and that the amendment referred only to the introduction of the decision of the minister of the 6th of August, 2001. The Prosecutor's claim of something existing before it was regulated by law, the decision of the 26th of June on the reestablishment of the posebna unit, all evidence shows that this was a unit which existed in the time of the Socialist Federative Yugoslavia. And in the transitional provisions, this is mentioned in the exhibit itself. The exhibit referred to by the Prosecutor represents only minor changes and amendments to the previous decision, rather than establishing the unit anew or establishing a new unit. In his oral closing arguments, the Prosecutor -- I do apologise. I've just received the transcript pages where General Jovanovski clarified the situation. That's 4894 to 4898, transcript pages 4894 to 4898. Supporting his arguments that something could exist de facto, although it did not exist de jure, the Prosecutor, again, refers to the testimony of witness M-052, who testified incorrectly about another issue before this Tribunal, which impeaches the credibility of this witness. On transcript page 11.017, he says that the Kuceviste reserve police station existed de facto, although it was created only at a later date. And when a written statement of Marjan Taskovski was put to witness M-052, where Marjan Taskovski confirmed that the police station existed only as of the 15th of August, 2001, M-052 made the comment quoted by my learned friend. However, Your Honours, the reserve police station of Kuceviste came into being on the 15th of August, and was opened on the 16th of August, 2001. In the binder we gave you yesterday, we included Exhibit P586, which is an overview of the payments of remuneration for the reserve force for this police station, reserve police station, Kuceviste. That's a letter from the Ministry of Interior, the sector for interior affairs Skopje, the Cair department, the Kuceviste reserve police station, dated September 2001. It includes a list of the persons which, as of the 16th of August, 2001 to the 31st of August, 2001 were engaged in this police station. This exhibit is in tab 17D. However, in tab 17E of yesterday's binder, you will find, Your Honours, part of the diary of witness M-084 or his log-book. This first lists the persons whose status in the reserve force was checked by witness Gjoko Popovski. However, on page N006-4709 -- so, N006-4709 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: 4715.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- of the text in English -- the pages are correct. I do apologise, Your Honours. I think I will never understand these e-court pages. That's ERN N006-4714. This contains a personal note of witness M-084, dated the 15th of August, 2001, referring to a meeting in the Ministry of Interior. That's -- well, what is important here is that at the end, it says that preparations are being carried out for the reserve police station. The last line says that: "On the 15th of August, preparations for the reserve stations were under way." And on the next page, Your Honours, there is an note, dated the 16th of August, 2001. That's N006-4715. The time is 7.30, and it says "opening of the reserve police station in Ljubanci." This evidence, Your Honours, confirms what the commander of this police station, Marjan Taskovski, wrote and what was put to witness M-052, and M-052 denied these indisputable facts. Attempting to prove his claim that there was effective control and that the de facto situation existed before the de jure situation came about, the Prosecutor refers to Exhibit P402, saying that parts of this exhibit show that the Lions existed before they were created in terms of legal documents. I wish to say the following, Your Honours: At a meeting of 29th of August, referred to by my learned friend, if we look at the exhibit in question, we shall see clearly that Mr. Boskoski addressed those present in connection with this issue, saying that the action of the Lions which were in the process of being established - this follows from Exhibit P74 and other exhibits in the file; Exhibit 1D61, referring to an amendments of the rules an organisation and work; and 1D62 - and the name Lions was given to this unit in these documents. It says that this will be the unit which, when the NATO forces leave Macedonia, will be able to take over the defence of Macedonia. Therefore, citing this conversation as a fact confirming their prior existence goes contrary to the gist of what Minister Boskoski said on the pages I quoted. Likewise, the following meeting, that -- or the next meeting that the Prosecutor relies on, that's Exhibit P402, must be seen in the same light. That is the meeting of the 10th of June which is about what is going to happen, not what has already happened. A complete clarification for this position was given by witness Zoran Jovanovski, who had been the deputy under-secretary for police at that time and later became under-secretary for police. However, the evidence speaks best, evidence and records: This is 1D59, that is government's decision; 1D60, president's decision on the establishment of this unit; then P74, which is the decision of the minister about the establishment of Lions; exhibits which create prerequisites for the establishment of this unit, 1D62 and 1D61; and the testimonies of all witnesses who stated that this unit became operational only in the autumn of 2001. The Prosecutor also refers to Exhibits P439 and 277. These are --

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Actually, I apologise, the Prosecutor cited only to P439. That is a video-clip in which it is mentioned that the Lions existed for eight months already. In relation to this, in the course of cross-examination and in course of the re-examination, the witness, General Jovanovski, provided a complete clarification. Actually, from the Exhibit P74, it is seen what was the procedure necessary in order to create the Lions, and it can be seen who will become part of the structure of the Lions. This exhibit presents clearly that parts of the posebna unit will become parts of the Lions. We know that this was a permanent unit that existed forever in the structure of the Ministry of Interior and also part of the reserve forces who will enter into contracts with the Ministry of Interior in the future. So, those individuals who will later become members of Lions have, as members of posebna or as members of the reserve forces, in their original police units participated in the fights, but as members of the posebna or members of the reserve forces. Probably, they became members of the Rapid Interventions Battalion, Lions, through the procedure that was followed. As explained by General Jovanovski, the words of the minister, when speaking to the Lions, that they fought bravely in the past six months refer to those who have been the best in the units and participated in the fights at those times, and not about the Lions that allegedly existed before and now were only formally established. So a proper overview of all evidence speaking about the establishment of the Lions unit and all testimonies speaking to this before this Court, we will find that the case and the theory of the Prosecutor presented in the closing arguments and today is absolutely unfounded. Clarifying the aforementioned video-recording, P439, General Jovanovski was also shown the video-clip that was Exhibit P277. They were both received in evidence; but on that occasion, General Jovanovski clarified another matter, and that was why are the brave young men called Lions and why was that title given to Lions once they were established as a unit. I already indicated that the title was given to the unit only on the 5th of September. The witness explained that that was part of the Macedonian history, and that in the old times the units that were fighting in the Ilinden uprising were called by that name. So nothing of it is related to the assertion of the Prosecutor that the Lions, either as a unit or as a group, existed before they were actually established, and no evidence within this procedure testifies to the opposite. In relation to this, what I just said can be found in Zoran Jovanovski's testimony on page 5.113, in relation to Exhibit P277, and 5.439 [as interpreted]. There is a mistake in the transcript. It is not "5.439" but "P439." Your Honours, I would speak briefly only about the issue raised today by my learned friend the Prosecutor, and that is whether the persons participating in the Ljuboten action had criminal background or not. We are all familiar because we are working in criminal matters that the procedure of resocialisation exists in all civilized countries in the world, and this is why the expunging of criminal records is not something that is known in the Macedonian penal legislation only. It exists everywhere in the world. But respectfully of this, we have accepted through the testimony of witness Vesna Dorevska two decisions of the constitutional court of the Republic of Macedonia that this requirement absence of prior convictions was removed from the law, or that was Exhibit P86. That was no longer a requirement for someone to become a member of the regular police forces. What is important for us here are the evidence that were on record and that we presented within your binders. They clearly show that the Prosecutor offered no evidence that would establish that any of the persons that allegedly on the 11th were issued weapons allegedly upon an order of Petre Stojanovski or Goran Mitevski, that was a list of eight individuals, that any of those had any criminal background; neither has the Prosecutor offered any evidence that would corroborate this; and neither has he offered anything that would corroborate such notions for the list from the PSOLO police stations. Individuals with criminal background in the words of the Prosecutor were actually villagers of Ljuboten village that were issued weapons on that day, and they were never brought in relation with anyone from the Ministry of Interior. But, at the end, Your Honours, as my learned friend said, the main issue here is that the Prosecutor failed to prove, firstly, that the persons who were prior perpetrators of crime have ever been or on that date members of the Ministry of Interior, and he offered no proof that they had been under effective command and control of Mr. Boskoski. So, our final position that we had presented before, as well, is that the minister took all necessary and reasonable measures be, all measures that he the detention unit to undertake according to the legislation of the Republic of Macedonia, and even measures that he had no duty to undertake but that he still undertook, wishing to elucidate events in and around Ljuboten and that they were appropriate in the given circumstances. So due to these reasons, we still remain, Your Honours, with the proposal that Mr. Boskoski is acquited on all counts of the indictment. And at the end, Your Honours, allow me to thank you, first of all, Your Honours, for providing, during the entire procedure, a situation where the Defence is able, in accordance with the principle of fair trial, to examine and question all witnesses that the Prosecutor offered, to examine a significant number of documents, and to call up witnesses that they considered appropriate and questioned them. Also, I wish to thank my colleagues from the Prosecutor's office who have demonstrated a significant degree of goodwill for cooperation to so that this procedure ran smoothly. I also thank, Your Honours, everyone, all members of the registry who also, as can be seen from numerous examples and situations, helped the Defence in presenting the evidence that it planned to present before this Court adequately. We also thank CLSS and all interpreters who often needed to manage the pace that the Defence took in order to use the time efficiently. I also thank all Macedonian interpreters who made efforts to adequately interpret the language that is not their native language, and also thank you, Your Honours, for allowing me to speak in my native language. And at the end, I wish to tell you that a huge part of the burden of the Defence presentation was carried by the Defence team, so I thank you the legal assistants, case managers, my consultants, and the interns without whom the Defence of Mr. Boskoski would not have been able to present its evidence as it did. I thank you, once again, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Residovic. Mr. Apostolski, do you need the lectern?

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I would ask for a moment, to take the lectern from my colleagues. Your Honours, on page 16 of today's transcript, the Prosecution claims that it is not changing its theory that there are some victims who were hors de combat, and it supports this claim by saying that in citing the law in their pre-trial submission. This is mentioned in paragraph 117 showing which persons are protected under Common Article 3. Nonetheless, in the indictment, in the pre-trial submission, as well as during the trial, it was claimed that all victims are civilians and not persons hors de combat. Your Honours, the fact that only three automatic rifles were brought and the evidence which irrefutably says that they were found in Ljuboten does not exclude the possibility that there were other weapons in the village of Ljuboten. The Prosecution itself, my learned colleagues from the Prosecution, in paragraph 68 of the indictment, lists - and Defence is in agreement with this - in paragraph 68 -- my apologies. I would like to rephrase my sentence. The Prosecution in the indictment in Article 68, lists Sunday, 12th of August 2001, the presence of armed Albanian combatants in Ljuboten was assessed at maximum ten to 15 persons armed with automatic weapons and at least one machine-gun. These individuals acted either alone or in small groups to prevent the advancement of the police units of Johan Tarculovski. The Prosecution claims that there were ten to 15 persons armed with automatic weapon there and at least one machine-gun. Furthermore, it is a fact that no house was searched, and the evidence, among which witness Bolton state that on the 14th of August, he found a gun in the Ametovski house, and that there is an proof that several guns were hidden in the Ametovski house. Your Honours, the Prosecutor claims that this was not a lawful anti-terrorist action because no special unit Tigers were used, nor the Lions were used in this action. At that time, unfortunately, the Lions did not exist, and the Tigers were fighting with the NLA and the Kosovo Protection Corps in Radusa, preventing the penetration from that direction to Skopje. It would be wonderful if Macedonia had multitude of units that could fight terrorists. However, Macedonia was not prepared for these terrorists. We're talking about a young state that fought with the courage of its defenders who were often volunteers or reservists. In fact, the reservists were the ones who destroyed the NLA in Vaksince and were most courageous on the ground. On page 22 of today's transcript, the Prosecution claims that I said yesterday that the Tribunal -- the prosecutors of the Tribunal in Macedonia checked the MOI, the courts, and the prosecutor's office of Macedonia, when they did not find the alleged participants in this action. This is not what I said yesterday. I said that the Prosecutors of the Tribunal carried out checks and asked criminal records of the alleged participants in the unit of Johan Tarculovski. To this end, they carried out checks in the MOI, the prosecutor's office of Macedonia, as well as in the courts of Macedonia, and they did not succeed in finding any single criminal record with a verdict for the alleged participants.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'm very sorry to interrupt, Your Honour. Just a point of clarification. What Mr. Apostolski is submitting right now, is this based on any evidence that has been admitted in this trial?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That, I think, is a question delivered to you, Mr. Apostolski.

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I just wanted to clarify that representatives from the Office of the Prosecutor of the Tribunal have been to Basic Court Skopje I, to Basic Court Skopje II.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is this a matter of evidence in this trial?

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this is not a matter of evidence on this trial. I'm just commenting --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, you shouldn't comment on matters that are not in evidence, Mr. Apostolski. Perhaps you should move on. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. The Prosecutor then claims that Tarculovski was the commander of the unit on the basis of evidence of witness M-052, their favourite witness, who had come to agreement with the Prosecution not to be accused in this case but, rather, to testify against Tarculovski. But I must say that (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: members of the Macedonian security forces enter the village. He reported to the minister in this action. He prepared the criminal reports against apprehended terrorists in the village who are now alleged victims. Witness M-052 is the one who did not want to speak the truth in front of this Tribunal, that he wanted and asked for his whole family to be dislocated outside of Macedonia, and that he would say anything in order to throw responsibility away from himself. Your Honours, once again, I propose that, after having considered the evidence, Mr. Tarculovski is acquitted of all points in the indictment. I would like to express my appreciation to the Court Chamber which very attentively followed our deliberations and allowed us a fair trial. It allowed the Defence to cross-examine witnesses with the aim of establishing the rightful factual situation. My appreciation and thanks to my colleagues of the Prosecution, to my colleagues of the Defence of Mr. Boskoski for their cooperation in this case, all with the aim to speed up the process and bring it to its end. I wish to point out also my appreciation to the registry for the cooperation we have had with them throughout the whole trial. Thank you, Your Honours, for permitting me to address this Chamber yet once again. I have nothing further to add.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Apostolski.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The Chamber is informed that each accused may wish to briefly address the Chamber. This is not a matter provided by the Rules, but the Chamber is prepared to allow that to occur, if the accused so wish. The Chamber could hear those brief comments now, conveniently. Is there any difficulty with that perceived by counsel? Ms. Residovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we have no comments, as we ask perhaps before our clients address, could you grant us a brief recess, and after that, they will address the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Our problem is with the tape mechanism. If we have a recess, it really needs to be half an hour because there must be a rewinding of the tapes, and there is an half an hour delay on the broadcasting, so it requires half an hour. If, for that reason, it would be much more convenient to proceed now, is there some particular concern you have that would require an adjournment?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we have no particular concern, but considering that those are the closing arguments presented by our colleagues, closing words, and, previously, you did accept such proposal to go in recess early. We could kindly ask you for this. But if the Chamber believes that there is any reason to not grant this proposal of the Defence, we will continue. But we believe that this would be more appropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The Chamber feels it is would be more practical for everybody to proceed now to hear what it is that each accused wishes to say. We would emphasise that this is an unusual procedure and the Chamber expects each accused to be brief in their comments, but we do appreciate that the accused may wish to put something finally to the Chamber. To that end, we would normally call upon Mr. Boskoski first, if that is convenient. Yes, Mr. Boskoski. Press the red button.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: THE ACCUSED BOSKOSKI: [Interpretation] Mr. President, Your Honours, first of all, allow me to express my high appreciation for giving me the opportunity, although this is not the usual practice, to say a few words at the end of this one-year process. After such a long period of absence after four years, thank you for giving me the opportunity to express my impressions and my pleasure at what transpired in the course of this process. In particular, Your Honours, I would like to point out that I agree fully with the clearly stated positions and arguments made by my esteemed team, who did not spare the efforts in the course of this last year to give their maximum with one and only goal before this Tribunal: Macedonia and international public state the truth about a very difficult time through which my country, the Republic of Macedonia, passed through. I also have to express my particular appreciation to my team that in this period of time, they worked exclusively on evidence based and founded on Macedonian law, international law, humanitarian law, so as to avoid any trace uncleared about this period through which the Macedonian state went through. Also, I would like to say that as a man, and as a minister at that time, Your Honours, at that time, for me, there was one high legal act important for me at that time: The constitution of the Republic of Macedonia, laws which I had to respect, rule books which I had to respect, a body of laws and regulations inherent to all modern and civilized states which seek to become member European associations above all NATO and the European Union. We're not a state which stands outside of this European system. We're not a state that works based on some fabricated rules. Our legal system is based on that of Europe and international experience. This is why at that time I did not and could not have any other alternative but to respect law of the Republic of Macedonia, and in accordance with my authorisations, to assist anyone and everyone who needed assistance. To those who requested such assistance from the ministry, I responded to this and I never differentiated among people along their ethnic, religious, or any other affiliation, not now, not in my past, not in my youth, because I, too, was born in an intermixed area. This is the intermixed and culturally different area where I was born. Mr. President, Your Honours, I worked in a most transparent manner. I was known as minister for this. I offered maximum assistance and help to this Tribunal as well. On several occasions, I met with Ms. Carla Del Ponte. We spoke about the difficult situation which Macedonia was facing and no one refutes this, because I knew that it would be this Tribunal where important decisions will be made which will contribute to the stabilization of our country, of our region as a whole, the region of south-eastern Europe. Your Honours, although thousands of days of loneliness have passed for me, much like those of Marques, I can say, Your Honours, that, nonetheless, I'm satisfied with everything I was given, including in this Tribunal believing in the sincerity of all participants in this process. Also, this is my only opportunity to thank the personnel at Scheveningen prison, among which I have discovered some secret talents, I must say. Although, we have been separated from those closest to us, from our family, from my beloved Macedonia, I remain steadfast and loyal and faithful and sure in one thing: That this Tribunal is just; that you will be prepared; after all the analysis that has been presented, you will be able to bring a just decision and acquit me from the points in the indictment. Ultimately, as a man, and this is the symbolic meaning of my name as well, I wish now to recall a great Macedonian, Mihail Rendzov, who said: "Dear Lord, for a while at least, choose some others. We are tired of death, we are no more prayers, we have no new blood for new victims." Let this Tribunal finalise these victims and the suffering and this message rendered by Rendzov which is embedded deeply also in the Statute of the Tribunal, which is bring reconciliation in my country and in the whole region. Let it bring about a normal life, breaking away from the past. I think this is a great role which the international community has endowed, and that this will be fulfilled. Once again, thank you very much for the attention you have given me, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Boskoski. Mr. Tarculovski.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: THE ACCUSED TARCULOVSKI: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I wish to thank you for giving me the opportunity, as well as giving it to my Defence team, to demonstrate that I have done no crime aiming against the civilians or civilian facilities. I have no objection in relation to the treatment that I received over the course of the trial. At the beginning, I was unlawfully arrested and I doubted that I would have a fair trial, but I wish to send a message to my immediate family that their support is my greatest treasure, and their love. Everything in life happens for a reason. I don't think that the three years spent in detention are time lost. I have learned many truths here. I learned not to be rushed, to be patient, to appreciate what I have, and to appreciate the differences. When my family grew larger, my life gained a completely different meaning. It's tragic and completely unnecessary what happened in Republic of Macedonia in 2001. It is tragic, and it is sad that some sick minds through perpetrating attacks against civilians, soldiers, and police officer fought for political offices. Your Honours, we, the Macedonians, are people of peace. We are always prepared to help anyone who needs it is most. No Macedonian wished for what happened in 2001. But nowhere, in no country in the world, would there be any one who would approve and support terrorist actions. It is a sacred duty for any individual to defend their country. I wish to give thanks for the support that the government of the Republic of Macedonia, headed by the prime minister, Nikola Gruevski, offers to me and my family. I'm also grateful to the Trial Chamber because I never felt during the trial as someone who was convicted already, or that I would be convicted because someone else wishes for this. Your Honours, this trial for my small but proud and biblical country, Macedonia, is a historical precedence. It would either give legitimacy to the legitimate Macedonian state institutions in the defence of the constitutional order or would reward the terrorists and encourage them in continuing their evil deeds. I thank you, and I believe your justness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tarculovski.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That concludes the hearing of evidence and submissions in this case, which has continued now for just over one year. The Chamber records its appreciation to counsel and their teams, to the court officers, interpreters, and the security personnel who have enabled the trial to be conducted with the convenience and efficiency that we have all enjoyed. It is now for the Chamber to give consideration to the very substantial amount of oral and documentary evidence it has received, and to the submissions that we have received in writing and now orally in the last three days. Inevitably that will take some time and the Chamber must reserve its decision before reaching a conclusion, as it must consider all those matters. That is what we will now do. We will now declare the case closed and reserve our decision.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 12.32 p.m.,
